s: has_duty_to relieve their widows [so the assembly is not burdened] Any believing man or woman who has widows in the family is told to relieve them. This keeps the assembly from being burdened so that it can relieve those who are widows indeed. Anyone who does not provide for his own, especially his household, has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.

l: care for widows and family obligations, 1 Timothy
s: A topic on supporting widows and family duties. Providing for one's own household is required, and neglect denies the faith. Relatives bear first responsibility; the assembly supports only true widows, age sixty and wife of one man, while younger widows are directed to marry, keeping the assembly unburdened.

l: honor and discipline of elders, 1 Timothy
s: requires public reproof of sinning elders [so the rest may fear] Elders who rule well receive double honor and wages, especially those who teach, and are shielded by the two-or-three-witness rule for accusations. Persistent sin is reproved publicly, and the instruction is to be carried out without prejudice or partiality. Hands are not to be laid hastily on anyone, and the text notes that some sins and good works are evident at once while others emerge later.

Bondservants living under the yoke are instructed to honor their masters fully so God's name and doctrine go unblasphemed; those with believing masters should not despise them as brothers but serve them even better.

may_be believing [some masters] Masters are to be honored by their bondservants. Believing masters are described as brothers who are believing and beloved and who partake of the benefit of the service.

A charge to the rich of the present age: avoid arrogance and trust in uncertain riches, hope instead in the living God, and be rich in good works, generous and ready to share, thereby storing a good foundation and gaining eternal life.

The love of money is called a root of all kinds of evil. Those determined to be rich fall into temptation, snares, and harmful lusts leading to ruin; in greed some stray from the faith and pierce themselves with sorrows.

This is the second letter to Timothy, written by Paul, an imprisoned apostle who knows his death is near. It is a personal and pastoral charge to Timothy, his beloved child in the faith, urging him to remain faithful and carry on the work. Chapter 1 opens with Paul's thanks for Timothy's sincere faith, which lived first in his grandmother Lois and mother Eunice. Paul urges him to stir up God's gift, since God gave a spirit of power, love, and self-control rather than fear. Timothy must not be ashamed of the Lord or of Paul the prisoner, because Christ abolished death and brought life to light through the Good News. Paul notes that all in Asia, including Phygelus and Hermogenes, turned from him, while Onesiphorus refreshed him and sought him out in Rome. Chapter 2 calls Timothy to be strong in Christ's grace, to entrust the teaching to faithful men who can teach others, and to endure hardship like a soldier, athlete, and farmer. Paul suffers to the point of chains, yet God's word is not chained. He quotes a trustworthy saying about dying, enduring, and reigning with Christ, warns against word-quarrels, and names Hymenaeus and Philetus as teaching error about the resurrection. Timothy is to flee youthful lusts, pursue righteousness, and correct opponents gently. Chapter 3 warns of grievous last days, when people will be lovers of self, money, and pleasure, with a form of godliness but no power. Timothy should turn from them, as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses. Contrasted with deceivers, Timothy has followed Paul's teaching and sufferings, including persecutions at Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra. He should continue in the God-breathed Scriptures he has known since infancy, which equip for every good work. Chapter 4 gives Paul's solemn charge to preach the word patiently, even as people seek teachers who please itching ears. Paul says he has fought the good fight, finished the course, and kept the faith, and a crown of righteousness awaits him. He asks Timothy to come soon with Mark, his cloak, and the books and parchments, since Demas deserted him and only Luke remains. He warns against Alexander the coppersmith, recalls the Lord standing by him at his first defense, and ends with greetings.

Paul is an apostle of Jesus Christ by God's will, appointed preacher and teacher of the Gentiles, who serves God with a pure conscience. The records follow him as a prisoner in chains for the gospel, enduring everything for the chosen ones so they may obtain salvation. He regards Timothy as his beloved child, reminds him of the teaching, conduct, faith, patience, love and steadfastness he followed, and commands him to preach the word. Paul recalls persecutions at Antioch, Iconium and Lystra, from which the Lord delivered him. Trust in God, who he is persuaded can guard what he committed, sustains him. As the account moves to its close, he describes himself as being offered, having fought the good fight, finished the course and kept the faith, and awaits a stored-up crown of righteousness. Personal details surround this: Demas abandoned him for love of this world, Luke alone is with him, Mark is useful for service, Tychicus was sent to Ephesus, his cloak was left with Carpus, Trophimus was left sick at Miletus, and Alexander the coppersmith did him much evil. At his first defense no one came to help, yet the Lord stood by and strengthened him.

Timothy is a beloved child of Paul, the addressee of a four-chapter letter (2 Timothy). He is remembered for sincere faith that first lived in his grandmother Lois and mother Eunice, and he has known the holy Scriptures from infancy. He holds God's gift, received through the laying on of Paul's hands, and is entrusted to guard a good thing through the Holy Spirit. Chapter 1 urges him to stir up his gift, not be ashamed, and endure hardship. Chapter 2 tells him to be strengthened in grace, commit teaching to faithful men who can teach others, serve as a good soldier, and handle the Word of Truth properly while pursuing righteousness, faith, love, and peace. Chapter 3 tells him to turn from corrupt men and remain in what he has learned. Chapter 4 solemnly charges him to preach the word, do an evangelist's work, and fulfill his ministry, then asks him to come to Paul soon, bringing Mark, the cloak, and the books, and to beware of Alexander.

God is portrayed in 2 Timothy as the Father of Jesus Christ, served by Paul with a pure conscience. He gives power, love, and self-control rather than fear, and saves and calls people according to his own purpose and grace. Chapter 1 stresses his ability to guard what is entrusted to him. Chapter 2 shows his word unchained despite imprisonment, his firm, sealed foundation, his knowledge of his own, and his granting repentance to opponents.

Jesus Christ is presented as Savior and Lord, descended from David and risen from the dead. In chapter 1, he appears as Savior, abolishes death, and brings life and immortality to light through the Good News, with grace given in him before eternal times. In chapter 2, he is the source of strengthening grace, the one believers die, live, and reign with, and he remains faithful even when people are faithless.

Onesiphorus is a loyal supporter of Paul: he often refreshed him, served at Ephesus, was unashamed of Paul's chain, and diligently sought him out in Rome. Paul prays for mercy on his house and for him on that day.

brings_to_light life and immortality The Good News is what Timothy is told to endure hardship for, according to God's power. Through it life and immortality were brought to light, and Paul was appointed as its preacher, apostle, and teacher of the Gentiles.
The gift of God is in Timothy through the laying on of Paul's hands, and Paul reminds him to stir it up. It is linked to the spirit God gave, one of power, love, and self-control rather than fear.

is_for Good News [Paul is not ashamed] Paul is a prisoner, with a chain of which Onesiphorus was not ashamed, and he suffers because of his appointment as preacher, apostle, and teacher. He says he is not ashamed, and he calls Timothy to share in enduring hardship for the Good News.

is_given_in Jesus Christ [before times eternal] God saved and called people with a holy calling, not according to their works but according to his own purpose and grace given in Christ Jesus before times eternal. This has now been revealed through the appearing of the Savior, who abolished death and brought life and immortality to light.
The Lord's servant is a figure who must be gentle, unquarrelsome, patient and able to teach, and who gently corrects opponents, hoping God grants repentance and recovery from the devil's snare.
Empty chatter is to be shunned because it advances ungodliness and spreads like gangrene; Hymenaeus and Philetus exemplify it, claiming the resurrection is past and overthrowing some people's faith.

The addressee is told to handle the Word of Truth properly, as a workman who doesn't need to be ashamed. Those who err concerning the truth, like Hymenaeus and Philetus, are contrasted with this, and opponents may come to a full knowledge of the truth.

Enduring hardship is urged on the addressee through the images of a good soldier, an athlete competing by the rules, and a laboring farmer. The speaker models it by enduring all things for the chosen ones, and the saying promises that those who endure will also reign with Christ.

contains vessels [gold, silver, wood and clay; some for honor, some for dishonor] A large house is used as an image containing not only vessels of gold and silver but also of wood and clay, some for honor and some for dishonor. It illustrates that a person who purges himself can become suitable for the master's use.

Vessels in the large house are of gold, silver, wood, and clay, some for honor and some for dishonor. Anyone who purges himself from these will be a vessel for honor, sanctified, suitable for the master's use, and prepared for every good work.

Lord Jesus Christ is the righteous judge of the living and the dead, before whom Paul gives his charge. He stands by and strengthens Paul, delivers him from evil, preserves him for his heavenly Kingdom, and at his appearing gives the crown of righteousness.

l: men of the last days (the corrupt men), 2 Timothy
s: The corrupt men of the last days are lovers of self, money, and pleasure rather than God, boastful, arrogant, disobedient, and unforgiving. They keep a form of godliness while denying its power, creep into houses and captivate gullible women, and oppose the truth as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses. Corrupted in mind and rejected concerning the faith, they will advance no further because their folly will be evident, yet they grow worse, deceiving and being deceived.

is_characterized_by grievous times They are announced as a time when grievous times will come. The period is marked by the rise of men with a long list of vices, including a form of godliness without its power.

Scripture is described as God-breathed and profitable for teaching, reproof, correction, and instruction in righteousness. Known from infancy, the holy Scriptures make one wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus, ultimately equipping believers completely for every good work.

affects all who desire to live godly in Christ Jesus The speaker recounts persecutions and sufferings at Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra, which he endured and from which the Lord delivered him. It is stated that all who desire to live godly in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution.

l: those who will not listen to sound doctrine, 2 Timothy
s: Group with itching ears, foretold by Paul, who reject sound doctrine, heap up teachers suiting their lusts, and ultimately turn from truth to fables.

Paul commands Timothy to preach the word, being urgent in season and out of season, reproving, rebuking and exhorting with all patience and teaching. It is tied to doing the work of an evangelist, and Paul recounts that through him the message was fully proclaimed so that all the Gentiles might hear.

is_a departure [time has come] Paul says he is already being offered and the time of his departure has come. He views it with confidence, having fought the good fight, finished the course and kept the faith, and expects the Lord to preserve him for his heavenly Kingdom.

is_given_by Lord Jesus Christ [on that day] Paul says the crown of righteousness is stored up for him, to be given by the Lord, the righteous judge, on that day. It is promised not to Paul only but to all who have loved Christ's appearing.

This is a pastoral letter from Paul, an apostle, to Titus, whom he calls his true child in a common faith. Paul left Titus in Crete to set things in order and appoint elders in every city. The letter moves from church leadership to community conduct to the basis of salvation. Chapter 1 lists the qualifications for elders: blameless, faithful husbands, with believing children, hospitable, self-controlled, and holding to sound doctrine. Paul warns of unruly deceivers, especially those of the circumcision, who upset households for dishonest gain. He cites a Cretan prophet's charge that Cretans are liars, evil beasts and idle gluttons, and tells Titus to reprove them sharply. Chapter 2 instructs Titus to teach what fits sound doctrine to older men, older women, younger women, younger men and servants, and to be an example himself. It grounds this conduct in God's grace, which brings salvation, teaches godly living, and looks for the appearing of Jesus Christ, who gave himself to redeem a people zealous for good works. Chapter 3 urges submission to rulers, gentleness toward all and readiness for good works. It recalls that God saved believers by his mercy, not their works, through the Holy Spirit's renewal, making them heirs of eternal life. Believers should avoid foolish disputes and a factious man after two warnings. Paul closes with travel instructions involving Nicopolis, Artemas, Tychicus, Zenas and Apollos, then greetings and a blessing.

Paul is a servant of God and apostle of Jesus Christ, entrusted with God's message by divine command. He writes to Titus, whom he left in Crete to set things in order and appoint elders, and instructs him to silence unruly deceivers and sharply reprove the Cretans.

Titus is Paul's true child in a common faith, greeted with grace, mercy and peace. Paul left him in Crete to set in order what was lacking, appoint elders in every city, and sharply reprove the Cretans so they become sound in the faith.

God, as portrayed in the Letter to Titus, is a truthful Savior who cannot lie and promised eternal life before time began. Chapter 1 shows him revealing his word through Paul's message, with overseers as his stewards and the defiled denying him by deeds. Chapter 2 says his grace has appeared bringing salvation to all, and his word must not be blasphemed by believers' conduct. Chapter 3 emphasizes his kindness and love toward mankind: not by works but by mercy, he saved believers through regeneration, poured out the Holy Spirit through Jesus Christ, and justified them as heirs of eternal life.

Jesus Christ is described as our great God and Savior, whose glorious appearing is the believers' blessed hope. He gave himself to redeem us from all iniquity and purify a people for his own possession, zealous for good works. Through him God richly poured out the Holy Spirit on believers.

Crete is the place where Paul left Titus so that he could set in order the things that were lacking. Elders are to be appointed in every city there. It is also where many unruly men, vain talkers and deceivers, are active.

has_reputation always liars, evil beasts, idle gluttons [stated by their own prophet; Paul affirms it as true] Cretans are characterized by one of their own prophets as always liars, evil beasts, and idle gluttons, and Paul says this testimony is true. Titus is told to reprove them sharply so that they may be sound in the faith and not pay attention to Jewish fables and commandments of men who turn from the truth.

l: elders (appointed in every city of Crete), Titus
s: Elders are officeholders Titus must appoint in every city of Crete under Paul's direction. They must be blameless, husband of one wife, with believing, well-behaved children, and free of anger, drunkenness, violence, greed. Hospitable, sober, holy, self-controlled, they hold the faithful word to exhort in sound doctrine and convict contradictors.

Unruly men in Crete are many: vain talkers and deceivers, especially of the circumcision. Their minds and consciences are defiled and unbelieving. They overthrow whole houses by teaching wrongly for dishonest gain, so their mouths must be stopped. They claim to know God yet deny him by deeds, being abominable, disobedient, and unfit for good work.
Sound doctrine is what the addressee is to speak about, with teaching fitted to each group. The doctrine of God our Savior is adorned by the good fidelity of servants.
Older men are instructed to be temperate, sensible, sober minded, then sound in faith, love, and perseverance, as stated in Chapter 2.
Older women are instructed to be reverent, avoid slander and excess wine, and teach what is good, culminating in training young wives to love their husbands and children.
Young wives are instructed, through training by older women, to love husbands and children and be sober-minded, chaste, kind, home-working and submissive to husbands, so God's word is not blasphemed.
should_be sober minded [exhortation] Younger men are to be exhorted to be sober minded.
Servants are exhorted to submit to their own masters, please in all things, not contradict or steal, and show good fidelity, thereby adorning the doctrine of God our Savior.

l: addressee (the one instructed to speak and exhort), Titus
s: The addressee is told to say what fits sound doctrine and to exhort the younger men and servants. He is to be an example of good works, showing integrity, seriousness, incorruptibility, and unconditionable speech, so that any opponent is ashamed. He is to speak, exhort, and reprove with all authority and let no one despise him.
The grace of God appeared bringing salvation to all men; it instructs believers to deny ungodliness and worldly lusts and live soberly, righteously, godly in this age, awaiting the blessed hope.

Salvation comes from God's kindness, love and mercy, not works of righteousness; it occurs through regeneration's washing and Holy Spirit renewal via Jesus Christ, justifying believers by grace as heirs of eternal life.

has_attribute good and profitable to men Good works are not the basis of salvation, since God saved the believers not by works of righteousness that they did. Yet believers are to be ready for every good work, to be careful to maintain them, and to practice them to meet necessary needs so they are not unfruitful. The text calls these things good and profitable to men.

The believers are a group addressed in Chapter 3, reminded they were once foolish, disobedient and deceived, but are now justified by grace and made heirs of eternal life. They are urged to obey rulers, be gentle and humble, do good works, shun foolish controversies, and avoid a factious man after two warnings. The passage ends with greetings and a blessing of grace.
Foolish controversies, including genealogies, strife and law disputes, are unprofitable and vain and must be shunned; a factious man ignoring two warnings is to be avoided as self-condemned.

This is the letter of 1 Peter, a five-chapter epistle written by Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, to chosen believers living as foreigners in the Dispersion across Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia. Its central concern is how believers should live faithfully, holy and hopeful, while suffering, with Jesus Christ as the model and basis of their salvation. Chapter 1 blesses God for causing believers to be born again to a living hope and a heavenly inheritance. Trials test faith like gold in fire. Readers are urged to be holy as God is holy, since they were redeemed by the precious blood of Christ, the lamb without blemish, and to love one another fervently. Chapter 2 tells them to put away wickedness and long for pure spiritual milk. Christ is the living stone and chief cornerstone, and believers are a spiritual house, royal priesthood, and holy nation. They are to behave well among the nations, submit to the king, governors, and masters, and honor all. Christ's unjust suffering, without sin or retaliation, is their example, and they have returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of their souls. Chapter 3 instructs wives and husbands in their conduct, with Sarah and Abraham as the example, then urges all to be like-minded and to bless rather than return evil. Suffering for righteousness is a blessing, and believers should answer for their hope with humility and a good conscience. Christ suffered once for sins, was made alive in the Spirit, preached to the spirits in prison from the days of Noah, and is now at God's right hand. Baptism is described as a symbol that saves through his resurrection. Chapter 4 calls believers to arm themselves with Christ's mind and abandon the lusts of the Gentiles. Because the end of all things is near, they are to be sober, loving, hospitable, and to serve one another with their gifts. They should not be astonished at the fiery trial, should rejoice in sharing Christ's sufferings, and should entrust their souls to a faithful Creator while doing good, since judgment begins with God's household. Chapter 5 has the author, a fellow elder and witness of Christ's sufferings, urge elders to shepherd God's flock willingly and as examples. The younger are to be subject to the elder, and all are to clothe themselves with humility. They are to cast their worries on God and resist the devil, who prowls like a roaring lion. The author prays that God will perfect and strengthen them after a little suffering. He names Silvanus as his scribe, sends greetings from the woman in Babylon and from Mark, and closes with a blessing of peace.
Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, writes to chosen ones living as foreigners in the Dispersion, blessing God, encouraging them in trials, and urging holiness, reverent fear, and fervent mutual love.

Jesus Christ is Lord, presented across five chapters of 1 Peter as the central figure of believers' faith. He was foreknown before the foundation of the world and revealed in this last age; his precious blood is likened to that of a lamb without blemish or spot. God raised him from the dead and gave him glory, which gives believers a living hope. He is described as a living stone, rejected by men but chosen by God, and as the chief cornerstone laid in Zion. Sinless and non-retaliating when cursed or abused, he committed himself to the one who judges righteously, and so left believers an example in suffering. He suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, bearing sins in his body on the tree to bring believers to God, so they might die to sins and live to righteousness. Put to death in the flesh but made alive in the Spirit, he preached to the spirits in prison who were disobedient in Noah's days. He is now at God's right hand in heaven, with angels, authorities and powers made subject to him. He is called the Shepherd and Overseer of souls, and the chief Shepherd who will be revealed to bring the crown of glory. Believers share his sufferings, will rejoice at the revelation of his glory, and glorify God through him; glory and dominion belong to him forever.

God, presented in 1 Peter as God the Father and Father of the Lord Jesus Christ, is holy, mighty, a faithful Creator, and the God of all grace. The records open with his mercy: he raised Christ from the dead, gave him glory, and caused believers to be born again to a living hope, electing them by foreknowledge and guarding them through faith. He calls them to holiness and judges each person's work without respect of persons. Next he chose the living stone, accepts believers' spiritual sacrifices through Jesus Christ, and called them out of darkness into his marvelous light as his own people. His will is that they silence foolish men by doing well, and he judges righteously and is to be feared. He values a gentle and quiet spirit, waited patiently in Noah's days, watches the righteous and hears their prayer, but sets his face against those who do evil. Later he supplies strength for service, is glorified through Christ, stands ready to judge the living and the dead beginning with his household, and is a faithful Creator to whom sufferers entrust their souls. It ends with him resisting the proud, giving grace to the humble, caring for his people, calling them to eternal glory, and perfecting and settling them after a little suffering, with glory and power ascribed to him forever.

l: chosen ones (recipients of the letter), 1 Peter
s: The chosen ones are the recipients of the letter: believers living as foreigners and pilgrims in the Dispersion across Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia. They are chosen according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, redeemed by the blood of Christ rather than silver or gold, healed by his wounds, and guarded by God's power through faith, with an incorruptible, undefiled inheritance reserved in Heaven. They love Jesus Christ though unseen. The records open by describing them as rejoicing amid trials and being called to holiness, fervent love, and obedient purity. Next they are described as living stones built into a spiritual house and holy priesthood, a chosen race, royal priesthood, holy nation, and people of God who have obtained mercy. As free people who are God's bondservants, they are to keep good behavior among the nations and abstain from fleshly lusts. They are then called to bless rather than repay evil, to inherit a blessing, and to be ready to explain their hope with humility and a good conscience. Finally they are told to leave their past Gentile lifestyle and live for God's will rather than human lusts. Facing a fiery trial and insults for Christ's name, they are called blessed, as partakers of Christ's sufferings with the Spirit of glory resting on them, and are told to entrust their souls to God while doing good.

Salvation, the salvation of souls, is ready to be revealed in the last time and received by believers through faith. Prophets diligently sought it and prophesied of its grace; angels desire to look into it. It brings redemption from empty ancestral ways by Christ's precious blood.

New birth is God's merciful act causing believers to be born again to a living hope through Jesus Christ's resurrection, from incorruptible seed, the enduring word of God, leading to an imperishable inheritance reserved in Heaven.

is_commanded_to chosen ones (recipients of the letter) [in all behavior] Believers are commanded to be holy in all their behavior, just as God who called them is holy, citing the scripture "You shall be holy, for I am holy." This calls for obedience as children of obedience, not conforming to their former lusts formed in ignorance. It is paired with reverent fear during their time as foreigners, and with sincere, fervent love for one another.

The Good News is the enduring word of the Lord, announced by the prophets' foretelling, then preached to the readers by preachers through the Holy Spirit sent from heaven, and something angels long to look into.

Suffering for doing good is presented as commendable with God when patiently endured, unlike punishment for one's own sin. Believers are called to it, following Christ's sinless, non-retaliating example. It is a fiery trial not to be wondered at, a share in Christ's sufferings in which to rejoice, and should be borne only as a Christian while continuing to do good and entrusting souls to God. Brothers worldwide undergo the same; it lasts a little while, then God perfects, establishes, strengthens, and settles them.

A teaching on submission to authority in Chapter 2: believers must submit to every human ordinance for the Lord's sake, to the king as supreme and to governors who punish evildoers and praise the good. Well-doing silences foolish men, and freedom is no cloak for wickedness. Servants must respect even wicked masters, and all honor everyone and the king.

Wives are instructed to submit to their own husbands so disobedient husbands may be won without words by pure conduct. Their adornment should be the hidden heart's gentle, quiet spirit precious to God, modeled by holy women and Sarah, who obeyed Abraham.
Husbands are instructed to live with wives according to knowledge, honor them as the weaker vessel and joint heirs of the grace of life, so that their prayers are not hindered.

Suffering for righteousness is a blessing for believers, who should not fear or be troubled. If God wills, suffering for doing right beats suffering for evil; Christ's suffering is the model, and accusers may be disappointed.

l: unbelievers (those who think it strange), 1 Peter
s: A group who think it strange that believers no longer join their excess, so they speak evil of them. They will give account to God, ready to judge the living and the dead; the text asks what awaits those disobeying the Good News.

begins_with believers (the addressees) [household of God] Judgment is coming from God, who is ready to judge the living and the dead, and the unbelievers will give account to him. The time has come for it to begin with the household of God, which raises the question of what will happen to the disobedient, the ungodly, and the sinner. The Good News was preached even to the dead so that they might be judged as men in the flesh but live to God in the spirit.

The elders are exhorted to shepherd the flock of God by exercising oversight voluntarily and willingly, not under compulsion or for dishonest gain. They are not to lord it over those entrusted to them but to be examples to the flock. When the chief Shepherd is revealed, they will receive the unfading crown of glory.

The author exhorts the elders as a fellow elder, a witness of Christ's sufferings, and one who will share in the glory to be revealed. He says he wrote briefly through Silvanus, whom he considers a faithful brother, to testify that this is the true grace of God. He sends greetings from the woman in Babylon and from Mark, whom he calls his son, and he closes with a blessing of peace.

The flock of God is the group among the readers that the elders are to shepherd, oversee, and set an example for. The text also addresses the younger ones to be subject to the elder and all to clothe themselves with humility and subject themselves to one another.
The devil is the believers' adversary, likened to a roaring lion prowling to devour; believers are urged to be sober, self-controlled, watchful, and to resist him steadfastly in faith.

Humility is commanded of all: they are to clothe themselves with it and subject themselves to one another, because God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble. Believers are told to humble themselves under God's mighty hand so that he may exalt them in due time.
